text: He is reading, and minding his own business, and she sits down anyway. From her first remark he has two options, be rude to a stranger or let the conversation run on her terms, and the film is built on the fact that most people take the second. Anthony Harvey shot it in Britain in 1967: fifty-five minutes, one subway car, two passengers. The brevity is structural. No subplot arrives, no third rider intervenes, and the exchange has to keep raising itself because nothing else has been provided to do. What begins as flirtation acquires a vocabulary about race and sex that neither party is improvising, since both have had these thoughts long before this ride. The escalation is not spontaneous on her side either. She has a method, and it shows in how seldom she needs to repeat a tactic.

The separation is recent, which is why the two of them still argue like people who share an address. Arnaldo Jabor's 1986 film puts a young Brazilian couple in a modern house and gives them a hundred and three minutes to go back through it. Everything the form usually supplies as relief, a walk outside, a friend at the door, has been withheld, so the pressure has nowhere to go but into the talk. Very little happens by way of incident and a great deal happens by way of position, since each is trying to fix the version of the past that will be carried out of the room. Neither is a villain, which removes the one thing that would make the conversation simple. Two faces, and a set of rooms bought for a future that has been cancelled.

The plot summary on file calls the film mannered and increasingly preposterous; IFFR's audience gave it their award. Giuseppe M. Gaudino follows a woman in her forties keeping two impossible arrangements running at once, a husband who is abusive and double-dealing, and a soap actor exactly as handsome and as plausible as a soap actor. Across 110 minutes the style refuses to behave. This is not a picture that observes its subject from a tactful distance; excess is the point of view, and the open question is whether that registers as a failure of taste or as an accurate report on how a life like hers feels from inside. The two verdicts on the record are arguing about precisely that. Italian, made in 2015, and entirely unembarrassed by melodrama.

Faust in a locked ward, with the tempter as a patient and the doctor no steadier than the men in his care. The bargain gets offered downward: an inmate promises an orderly, innocent and not clever, more money than he can picture in exchange for help getting out the door. Peter Ustinov, directing in America in 1972, plays that for comedy without ever quite dropping the older and colder version of the story underneath, so the 108 minutes keep changing which one is in force. The Silver Bear for leading performance on its record points at the imbalance the writing runs on: the mad man is given all the good lines and the sane one almost none. The setting handles the rest. In a hospital, nobody's account of himself counts for very much.

A Slovene boy and a German girl walk out of a bombed town together, and the man who falls in with them on the road is a Black American pilot who has just come down out of the sky. That is 1957, in Yugoslavia, in Slovene, a war film made twelve years after the war by people who had it in their own fields, and the casting alone marks what France Štiglic was prepared to put on a screen. The three have German in common and not much else, plus a rumour of a valley the fighting never reached. American planes killed the boy's parents. He takes to the pilot anyway, and Štiglic sets that contradiction down early and declines to tidy it. Eighty-two minutes, the adults mostly offscreen, and a destination that exists first as something the children have been told about.

In 1955 a British audience knew exactly what an RAF pilot had been ten years earlier, and what he might be now that nobody needed him to fly. That knowledge does much of the work here. A judge's wife, comfortable and bored past bearing, leaves a husband whose profession is the delivery of measured sentences for a man who lives at a rhythm she first mistakes for vitality. Anatole Litvak keeps the whole thing domestic. The 98 minutes go not to whether she was right to leave, which the film treats as settled, but to the discovery that no household can absorb the man she left for. Sympathy is distributed unusually evenly, which is what makes the situation feel closed rather than tragic. The judge is not a monster. He is dull, and dullness is a harder thing to leave than cruelty.

Sibilla Aleramo and Dino Campana were poets, and Michele Placido's film gives its ninety-six minutes to what they did to each other rather than to what they wrote. That is a real decision. It skips the apprenticeship and the reputation and stays with the daily conduct of two people whose work requires solitude and whose attachment will not permit it. What the camera watches is scheduling: whose day gets interrupted, who travels to whom, which of them can afford to be unwell this week. Laura Morante and Stefano Accorsi take the parts, and the European Film Award for Best Actress that came of it describes the centre of gravity accurately. The film stays with the woman trying to keep working while being loved badly, and treats the man less as her subject than as the weather she writes in.

A man took the blame for a crime a woman committed, and she left rather than live beside what it cost him. Years pass. They meet again inside ordinary adult lives, work and other people and the routines that filled the interval, and Cai Shangjun gives much of his 131 minutes to those routines rather than to the reckoning they imply. The pacing is the argument. What happened is not a puzzle to be solved but a weight the two carry differently: one wants to be forgiven, the other wants to be let go, and neither can hand over what the other is asking for. This is a Chinese production of 2025 whose idea of a scene is two people in the same room with incompatible accounts of why. Two hours and eleven minutes of being careful around each other is not the delay before the film; it is the film.

He practices law, she translates books, and the noise from the street has begun to shape their evenings. Brooklyn Heights, 1971: a couple in middle age with money, no children, and a marriage that has quietly turned into an arrangement for sharing rooms. Frank D. Gilroy keeps two irritations running at the same level and refuses to rank them, the vandalism and the break-ins on one side, the fact that neither of them has anything left to say on the other, until the fear coming from outside and the fear coming from the dinner table are hard to tell apart. Ninety-seven minutes, mostly interiors, almost no plot in the usual sense. Everything rides on the way a woman looks at her own furniture, and on how long the two of them can keep calling the situation manageable.

Blindness arrives by accident; the second injury arrives from the people who love him. Raymond's family starts speaking to him the way adults speak to a child who has been ill, which is a form of care and also a demotion. Georges Lacombe made it in France in 1951, and his subject turns out to be instruction rather than affliction: a nun from a centre where blind people learn Braille takes Raymond on, and the fingers-on-paper business of the alphabet becomes the plot, something to be mastered at an age when mastering things was supposed to be finished. Across 110 minutes the question is never whether he will see again. It is whether he will be allowed to work, to decide, and to be addressed in the register he was addressed in before.

Nadia is fifteen and a Communist, not as an opinion she arrived at but as the house she was raised in: Polish parents, meetings, the whole inheritance. Paris, 1952. Police beat her at a demonstration against the Americans, a photographer from Match carries her out of it, and her politics acquire a complication with a face. Véra Belmont runs a second line beside the first, in which her mother's lover from before the war returns from Siberia with scars and with news about Stalin that the French comrades would rather not hear. One faith, tested at two ages. What sharpens the film is that the pressure on Nadia is social before it is ideological: her own comrades begin discussing whether she can stay, and at fifteen, expulsion means losing every person she eats with.

A prep class in central Paris, a football pitch, and a family in the suburbs who are told some of it. Fatima is seventeen, the youngest daughter of a French-Algerian household, and the year she leaves school for the course that decides French futures is also the year she has to work out how much of herself to give to whom: a boyfriend her parents know nothing about, an attraction to women she has confided to no one. Hafsia Herzi declines to build a crisis out of that. The 112 minutes go to management instead, what is said at the table, what is said in the car, which friend gets which version, and the strain comes from Fatima's care for the people she is not telling. It took the Louis Delluc Prize, and the fit is exact: the film keeps its voice down and never treats her caution as a symptom.

Most films about a marriage pick a crisis and stay inside it; this one picks the quiet stretches and keeps returning to them across years. John and Abby Edwards marry in New York around the turn of the century, and Irving Reis, filming in 1952, checks in on them periodically, leaving whatever changed in the gaps to be read off the two of them rather than explained. That puts an unusual load on the photography, and the Academy Award the film took for black-and-white cinematography is less a decoration than a description of where the work went: with little incident to stage, light and lens carry the passing of time. It runs 103 minutes and moves between comedy and something considerably drier. A long marriage is mostly small adjustments, and a film willing to shoot only those has to make each one legible.

A farm on the Moldau, a daughter who watches the river head somewhere she has never been, and Prague at the other end of it. Anna Jobst's father is rich, conservative and settled; her wish is the smallest available rebellion, which is to see the city the water is going to. The river is the only real machinery in the story, since it makes leaving look less like a break than like following something. Veit Harlan gives that 110 minutes and a shape as old as any ballad: departure, the wrong company, the reckoning. The year is the difficulty. This was made in Germany in 1942, and a story whose arithmetic runs country-good, city-ruinous, obedience-safe is arithmetic with obvious uses. Watching it now means watching two things at once, a farm girl's story and the work that story was being asked to do.
